Yes. After adjustment for the other six background columns, the men with aid had a lower rate of re-arrest. The p-value is just below alpha 0.05, and the top of the confidence interval is close to 1, so the evidence is weak.

- **Effect size:** the hazard ratio for financial aid is **0.684 (95% CI 0.470 to 0.996)**, two-sided **p = 0.0474**.

1. **Data check:** the file has 432 rows and 432 men, one row per man. Each man is one replicate. No values are missing. The arrest column holds 1 for re-arrest and 0 for no re-arrest by the end of follow-up. In total, 114 men were re-arrested (26.4%).

3. **Cox model** with these covariates: fin, age, race, wexp, mar, paro and prio. It used the Efron method for tied times and all 432 men with 114 re-arrests. No rows were dropped.

|---|---|---|
| Re-arrested | 66 (30.6%) | 48 (22.2%) |
| Not re-arrested at 26 weeks | 0.852 | 0.898 |
| Not re-arrested at 52 weeks | 0.694 | 0.778 |

- At 52 weeks, the difference is 8.3 percentage points in favor of aid.
- Log-rank test: chi-square 3.838, df 1, p = 0.0501. At alpha 0.05 this is not significant.

| Covariate | Hazard ratio | 95% CI | p |
|---|---|---|---|
| fin | 0.684 | 0.470 to 0.996 | 0.0474 |
| age (per year) | 0.944 | 0.904 to 0.986 | 0.00903 |
